raw_response:
I've been working this land since I was twenty years old. My father farmed before me. I know this soil the way I know my own hands.

My 7.7 mu I split two ways. Five mu for the wheat-maize rotation — that's the big plot by the canal. The other 2.7 mu I put to cotton, the plot closer to the well because cotton needs water more often and I don't want to drag the pipe so far.

**Wheat** goes in October. I buy certified seed from the township supply station — the neighbors who tried the new Jimai variety last year all got better yields than me, so I'm switching to that this year. Before I plow I spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu — 50 kg, the 15-15-15 kind. After the New Year when the weather warms, I go out and broadcast 10 kg of urea per mu by hand. Three waterings I never skip: the winter water before the ground freezes, the jointing water in April, and the heading water in May. Miss one and you lose a hundred jin per mu easy. I spray twice — once when the aphids come in spring, once if I see rust spots on the leaves.

**Maize** I plant the day after wheat harvest, sometimes the same afternoon if my son helps me. I run the rotary tiller once quickly, no need to deep plow. I use hybrid seed — everyone does now, you'd be a fool not to. I throw down 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base, then when the plants reach my knee I add 15 kg urea. If August is dry I water twice. One spray for corn borer, maybe two if it's bad.

**Cotton** gives me the most worry and the most work. Topping, removing suckers, watching for bollworm — it never rests. But it brings cash when prices are decent. I put two bags of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, then add urea three times during the season — about 8 kg each time. Cotton that runs short of food during flowering drops its bolls and that's money gone. Four waterings, sometimes five if July is hot and dry. I spray for bollworm four times. No choice — if you let it go one round the whole crop is finished.

I do what I did last year, mostly. Costs are going up — urea was cheaper before. But I would rather spend an extra hundred yuan on fertilizer than come up short on harvest and not have enough to sell. A bad harvest means I can't pay the water fees and my daughter's school money gets tight. So I don't cut corners on the inputs.
